title: The treaty and Kashmir
hookLine: Punjab loses land, and Kashmir is sold to Gulab Singh

cards: No guns this time. A table, papers, ink, men in good coats. On one side, British officials.
On the other, ministers speaking for a boy Maharaja who isn't old enough to read what's being signed. The British army is camped at Lahore. Everyone at that table knows who won at Sobraon.
What's left is to write down what it will cost. Land the Khalsa held is about to change hands without a shot.

teach.b: Under the treaty of Lahore, the kingdom gave up the fertile country between the Beas and the Sutlej rivers. The old river line Ranjit Singh had kept was pushed back into the heart of the Punjab.
The Khalsa army was cut down in size, and British troops stayed in Lahore.

teach.h: A PAYMENT THAT COULDN'T BE MET.
teach.b: The British also demanded a large payment for the cost of the war. The treasury in Lahore couldn't meet it, so in place of the money, the British took Kashmir and the hill country around it.
Then, in a second treaty at Amritsar, they sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh, the Dogra raja of Jammu. You met him at the court of many faiths, one of the Dogra brothers who served the Maharaja.

In the war he had kept out of the fighting and acted as a go-between with the British. Now he became ruler of the valley the Sikh army had once climbed the passes to win. Kashmiris themselves were not asked.
Sobraon was a battlefield, and Sikh memory honors the men who fell there.
The treaty is remembered differently: as a loss made quietly, by signatures, with a raja who had served the court walking away as ruler of Kashmir.
Some losses don't happen in the fight. They happen afterward, on paper, while the people affected aren't in the room.

how: Sikh histories remember the treaties after the war with the British as a loss made on paper, in which the Punjab gave up land and Kashmir passed to Gulab Singh.

o: a treaty, a peace made with ink, not swords
a truce that pauses a war for a festival
a ransom paid to free soldiers taken in battle

games.q: what the treaty took — tap the pairs.
p: the Dogra raja who bought Kashmir

s: Kashmir was won by the British in battle
it was taken in place of a payment Lahore couldn't meet, then sold to Gulab Singh.
Gulab Singh had served at the Maharaja's court
he was one of the Dogra brothers; in the war he acted as a go-between.
the treaty left the Lahore kingdom's land untouched
it gave up the country between the Beas and the Sutlej.

games.q: you're the British, after Sobraon. you've taken Kashmir in place of money Lahore can't pay. what do you do with the valley?
o: sell it to Gulab Singh, the Dogra raja of Jammu.
games.why: in a second treaty at Amritsar, the British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh; Kashmiris themselves were not asked.

practice: Bring to mind something you lost because of a decision made somewhere else, a job cut in a meeting you weren't in, a move you didn't pick, and notice it without arguing, your breath slow and even.
Then notice one thing that's still yours, that no table could sign away, and rest there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi, a treaty, a peace made with ink rather than swords: land given up after the war, and the valley taken in place of money and sold to Gulab Singh.

orig.note: sandhi, a treaty; a peace made with ink rather than swords.

carryVoice: Your line: lost at a table. Ink can move a border as surely as guns. Until tomorrow.
